message.content:
**Atomic‑mass units (amu)**  
| Particle | Mass (amu) |
|----------|------------|
| **Proton** | \(m_p \approx 1.007\,276\,466\,879\;\text{u}\) |
| **Neutron** | \(m_n \approx 1.008\,664\,917\,020\;\text{u}\) |

These values come from CODATA 2018/2022 compilations and include the current best‐fit uncertainties (≈ \(±2\times10^{-11}\,\text{u}\)).

---

### Effective “diameter” of a nucleon  

A nucleon's spatial extent isn’t sharply defined because it’s a quantum object bound by the strong force. Experimental determinations usually quote a *root‑mean‑square* (rms) charge or matter radius rather than a hard surface. Converting those radii into a rough “effective diameter” gives:

| Particle | rms radius (fm) | Approximate diameter (fm) |
|----------|-----------------|---------------------------|
| **Proton** | \( r_{\!p}^{\rm rms} \simeq 0.840\, - 0.875\;\text{fm}\) | \( d_{p} \simeq 1.68\, - 1.75\;\text{fm}\) |
| **Neutron** | \( r_{\!n}^{\rm rms} \simeq 0.870\, - 0.930\;\text{fm}\) | \( d_{n} \simeq 1.74\, - 1.86\;\text{fm}\) |

Typical literature quotes a single representative number such as **~1.7 fm** for either nucleon when speaking informally about their “size.” If you need a more precise figure for a specific calculation, use the full rms radius values above and remember they refer to probability distributions, not sharp boundaries.
